5.1.1:
Why this matters

5S (1.4.5) is easy to start and easy to lose. Most organizations have done a "big clean-up" that looked great for a month and then slid back. The Control phase is about making improvements stick, and for 5S that means building routines that keep the workplace organized without heroic effort.

The big idea

5S decays unless something actively holds it in place. The last two S's, Standardize and Sustain (Self-discipline), exist exactly for this, and the control methods below put them into practice. If a 5S area has slipped back, the failure is almost always in Sustain.

Control methods

1. Audits and scored checklists.
A short checklist covers each S ("Only needed items at the workstation? Every tool on its shadow? Floor clean, no leaks? Standards posted and current?"). Each item is scored (for example 0 to 4), giving a total 5S score that can be tracked over time. Scores are posted visibly, and low scores trigger action, not blame.

2. Visual controls.
Make the standard and any deviation obvious at a glance:

  • Floor markings: lanes, pallet locations, keep-clear zones.
  • Shadow boards: an empty outline shows a missing tool immediately.
  • Labels and color codes: every location named; a place for everything.
  • Photos of the standard: "this is what right looks like".
  • Min/max lines on shelves and bins.

3. Standard work and ownership.
Each area has a named owner and a written routine: who does what cleaning and checking, how often. When everyone owns it, no one does.

4. A regular schedule.

  • Daily: quick operator checks (5 minutes at shift end).
  • Weekly: area leader audit.
  • Monthly or quarterly: management audit or walk, which shows that leaders care.

Management attention is the single strongest sustainer: what leaders check, people keep doing.

Worked example

A dock was 5S'd in March, scoring 92%. By July it scores 58%: tools left out, pallets in walkways, labels missing. Sort, Straighten and Shine were clearly done once. What failed was Sustain: no regular audits, no owner, no leadership walks. The fix: assign an area owner, add a daily 5-minute end-of-shift check, post weekly scores, and include the dock in the monthly management walk.

Check yourself

  1. 5S gains faded within months. Which S failed?
  2. Name three visual controls.
  3. Why does every 5S area need a named owner?
  4. What does a scored audit add beyond "looks clean"?
Show answers
  1. Sustain (Self-discipline).
  2. Any three of: floor markings, shadow boards, labels, color codes, photos of the standard, min/max lines.
  3. Shared responsibility tends to mean no one takes action; an owner is accountable for keeping it up.
  4. A consistent, comparable measure over time that shows decay early and focuses attention.

Key takeaways

  • 5S decays without active control; decay means Sustain failed.
  • Controls: scored audits and checklists, visual controls, standard work with area owners, a daily/weekly/management schedule.
  • Leadership attention sustains 5S.
5.1.2:
Why this matters

Kanban is the practical mechanism behind pull (1.4.1). It keeps inventory and work in process low and visible, prevents overproduction, and makes the system self-regulating: nothing is made or moved until it is needed.

The big idea

A kanban (Japanese for "signboard" or "card") is a signal that authorizes a process to produce or move a specific quantity, only when the next step has used something. No signal, no production. The signal can be a card, an empty bin, a marked floor space, or an electronic message.

Types of kanban

  • Production kanban: authorizes a process to make a quantity to replace what was taken.
  • Withdrawal (move, conveyance) kanban: authorizes moving a quantity from a storage point to the user.

Supermarkets and two-bin systems

  • A supermarket is a small, controlled store of items between processes. The downstream process "shops" (takes what it needs); the upstream process restocks only what was taken, signaled by kanban.
  • A two-bin system is the simplest kanban: parts are used from bin 1; when it is empty, it becomes the signal to refill, while work continues from bin 2. Common for fasteners, packaging, office supplies, spare parts.

The rules of kanban

  1. The downstream process pulls (withdraws) only what it needs, when it needs it.
  2. The upstream process produces only what was withdrawn, in the order the kanbans arrive.
  3. No defects are passed on. A defective item stops the flow and gets attention.
  4. Nothing moves or is made without a kanban.
  5. Level the load (heijunka) so demand on upstream processes is steady.
  6. Reduce the number of kanbans over time: fewer kanbans mean less inventory, and the problems the extra inventory was hiding become visible and can be fixed.

How many kanbans?

N = (demand × lead time × (1 + safety factor)) ÷ container size

Always round up to the next whole kanban.

  • Demand: usage per time period.
  • Lead time: time to replenish one container (in the same time unit as demand).
  • Safety factor: extra buffer for variation (for example 0.2 = 20%).
  • Container size: quantity per kanban.

Worked example. A dock uses 200 stretch-wrap rolls a day. Replenishment takes half a day. Safety factor 20%. Rolls come in cases of 25.

N = (200 × 0.5 × 1.2) ÷ 25 = 120 ÷ 25 = 4.8 → 5 kanbans (5 cases circulating).

CONWIP (recognition only)

CONWIP (constant work in process) caps the total work allowed in a whole line rather than item by item: a new job starts only when one finishes. Low exam yield.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Kanban authorizes production or movement only after downstream consumption.
  • Round the number of kanbans up.
  • Production kanban = make; withdrawal kanban = move.
  • Fewer kanbans over time, not more.

Check yourself

  1. What does a kanban authorize?
  2. Demand 600 per day, lead time 0.25 day, safety factor 10%, container 40. How many kanbans?
  3. What is a two-bin system?
  4. Why reduce the number of kanbans over time?
  5. Which kanban type authorizes moving parts from a supermarket to the line?
Show answers
  1. Producing or moving a specific quantity, only to replace what was used downstream.
  2. (600 × 0.25 × 1.1) ÷ 40 = 165 ÷ 40 = 4.125, round up to 5.
  3. Two containers: when the first empties, it signals replenishment while the second is used.
  4. To lower inventory and expose the problems excess inventory was hiding.
  5. A withdrawal (move) kanban.

Key takeaways

  • Kanban = a pull signal; nothing is made or moved without one.
  • Production vs withdrawal kanbans; supermarkets and two-bin systems.
  • Rules: downstream pulls, make only what was taken, no defects passed on, level the load.
  • N = demand × lead time × (1 + safety) ÷ container size, rounded up.
5.1.3:
Why this matters

People make mistakes, no matter how trained or careful. Training, warnings and inspections help, but they rely on attention, which fails. Poka-yoke designs the process so that mistakes cannot happen, or are caught immediately. It is one of the strongest controls in the Control phase because it does not depend on anyone remembering.

The big idea

Poka-yoke (Japanese for "mistake-proofing", developed by Shigeo Shingo at Toyota) separates errors from defects:

  • An error is a mistake (picking the wrong part, skipping a step).
  • A defect is the bad result that reaches the customer.

Errors may be inevitable, but defects are not, if the process catches the error at the moment it happens and before it becomes a defect.

Two levels of strength

  1. Control (prevention) type: makes the error impossible, or stops the process when it occurs.
  • A fuel nozzle for diesel that does not fit a gasoline tank.
  • A fixture that accepts a part in only one orientation.
  • A truck that will not start until the seat belt is fastened, or a liftgate that will not lower unless the truck is in park.
  • Software that will not let you submit an order without a delivery address.
  1. Warning (detection) type: makes the error immediately obvious, alerting a person to act.
  • A beeper for an open door, a light when tire pressure is low.
  • A scanner that beeps red when the wrong item is picked.
  • A checklist with a missing-item alarm.

Prevention is stronger than warning, because warnings can be ignored.

Three methods of detection

  • Contact method: detects shape, size, position or color by physical or sensor contact. "Does the part touch the limit switch?" Guide pins, keyed connectors, sensors.
  • Fixed-value (counting) method: checks that a set number of actions or parts is complete. A kit tray with exactly 12 pockets: any empty pocket shows a missing part. Counters that require 8 bolts before release.
  • Motion-step (sequence) method: checks that steps are done in the right order. Systems that will not proceed until the previous scan or step is confirmed.

Source inspection

Traditional inspection checks finished products (judgment inspection): it only finds defects after they are made. Shingo's approach favors source inspection: checking the conditions that cause errors at their source, before the operation, plus 100% automatic checking at the point where errors happen. Poka-yoke devices make 100% checking cheap.

Worked example

Problem: wrong paperwork sometimes goes with a trailer (shipping documents for another load).

  • Warning: the yard scanner beeps if the bill of lading barcode does not match the trailer's barcode.
  • Prevention: the gate system will not release the trailer until the bill of lading and trailer barcodes match.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • A fixture that accepts parts in only one orientation = prevention (control) type.
  • Alarms and lights = warning (detection) type.
  • Prevention beats warning.
  • Contact, fixed-value, motion-step: the three methods.
  • Poka-yoke is associated with Shigeo Shingo.

Check yourself

  1. What is the difference between an error and a defect?
  2. A connector that only plugs in one way: which type?
  3. A kit tray with a pocket for every part: which method?
  4. Why is prevention preferred to warning?
  5. What is source inspection?
Show answers
  1. An error is the mistake; a defect is the bad result. Poka-yoke stops errors from becoming defects.
  2. Control (prevention) type, contact method.
  3. Fixed-value (counting).
  4. Warnings rely on people noticing and acting; prevention makes the error impossible.
  5. Checking the conditions that cause errors at their source, before they produce defects.

Key takeaways

  • Poka-yoke (Shingo): make errors impossible or immediately obvious.
  • Control/prevention type (stronger) vs warning/detection type.
  • Methods: contact, fixed-value (counting), motion-step (sequence).
  • Source inspection and 100% automatic checks at the point of error.
